data.title: 381 DAYS
data.subtitle: Montgomery, Alabama, 1955–1956
data.introBody: December 1955. Montgomery, Alabama. Rosa Parks has been arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a city bus. By morning, the Black community will know. You are a domestic worker — you ride that bus every day to reach your employer's house across town. Now you must decide, day by day, how you will live inside a movement that is asking everything of ordinary people.
data.trailFeedOpener: December 5, 1955: the first day of the boycott. The buses roll past, nearly empty.

resourceLabels.weeklyWages: The cash in your purse — what you earn and what you have left to spend on food, shoes, and emergencies.
resourceLabels.standing: Your reputation among neighbors, church members, and the boycott community — how much they trust you and how openly you walk with them.
resourceLabels.endurance: The reserve in your body and spirit — how much the miles, the hours, and the pressure have worn you down.

events.title: Week Two of the boycott — your feet are blistered and your employer, Mrs. Hartley, meets you at the door earlier than usual. She has heard talk. She looks at you with an expression you cannot fully read: part worry, part warning.
events.text: Mrs. Hartley says, 'Ida, I need to ask you something and I need the truth. Are you walking all this way because of that boycott? Because I want you to know I can arrange a ride — my neighbor's colored girl is still riding. I don't want any trouble here, and I don't want you worn out. But I need to know what's going on under my roof.' She is your income, your reference, the reason you can pay your sister's doctor bills. She is also the roof the movement is marching out from under.

choices.text: Look at her steadily and say: 'Yes, ma'am. I'm walking because I won't ride until we're treated right. I'll still do my work. But I won't take that ride.'
choices.result: She chose to be known — to let the cost fall where it may rather than hide the truth of who she is inside the house where she labors.

choices.text: Drop your eyes and say: 'My feet don't mind it, Mrs. Hartley. The mornings are cool. No need to trouble anyone for a ride.' You say nothing else.
choices.result: She chose to remain unseen — holding the line between what she carries inside and what the world is allowed to know about her, for reasons the world cannot easily judge.

events.title: 52,000 Flyers in a Night
events.text: Jo Ann Robinson's Women's Political Council has mimeographed 52,000 boycott notices and needs help distributing them before dawn. Your neighborhood is on the list. You have blistered feet and a long workday tomorrow.
events.imageSearchQuery: Jo Ann Robinson Women's Political Council Montgomery

choices.text: Walk the whole neighborhood. Every door gets a flyer.
choices.result: You are out until three in the morning. Your feet ache and your candle gutters. By dawn, every door on your block has a flyer. Neighbors nod at you differently the next day.

choices.text: Take your block and go home. Enough for one night.
choices.result: You do your part and sleep. A reasonable choice. The flyers still go out — your block and the next, done by others who stayed longer.

choices.text: You are too tired. Leave the stack at the church steps.
choices.result: The stack sits in the cold until someone else moves it. You rest, but a neighbor who spots the pile sees your name on the sign-up sheet — and doesn't say anything.

trivia: Jo Ann Robinson mimeographed the first 52,000 boycott flyers in a single night before the boycott began.
The Women's Political Council had been planning a bus protest for months before Rosa Parks's arrest provided the right moment.

events.title: The Mass Meeting at Dexter Avenue
events.text: E.D. Nixon and the newly chosen Reverend King have called a mass meeting at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church. Five thousand people are outside; the church holds a thousand. You made it inside. When the call for open testimonials comes, people are waiting to hear from the domestic workers.
events.imageSearchQuery: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church Montgomery Alabama

choices.text: Stand and speak. Tell them what the walk already costs.
choices.result: Your voice shakes at first. You describe the blisters, the miles, the employer's watching eyes. The room is very quiet, then very loud. Afterward, three women you have never met take your hands. Your sister, who came, looks at you like she does not entirely know you.

choices.text: Stay seated. Listen. Take it all in.
choices.result: You hear King speak for the first time about love and dignity and the long arc of justice. It fills something in you. No one knows you were here, but you were.

choices.text: Leave early. You have a long morning ahead.
choices.result: You slip out before the vote. You hear from neighbors later that the crowd voted unanimously to continue the boycott. You were not part of that vote.

trivia: The first mass meeting was held at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church on December 5, 1955 — the same day as the first boycott.
E.D. Nixon was an NAACP chapter president and Pullman porter who bailed Rosa Parks out of jail and pushed for a mass meeting.

sageAdvice.name: E.D. Nixon
sageAdvice.role: NAACP chapter president and Pullman porter
sageAdvice.line: You are not here to be comfortable. You are here because somebody has to stand up first.

image.searchQuery: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church Montgomery Alabama

events.title: The Carpool Dispatch Problem
events.text: The MIA has set up a carpool system, but it is stretched thin. A neighbor who has a car works on your shift and could take three more women — but she needs someone reliable to coordinate pickup times and keep drivers honest. That someone could be you.

choices.text: Take on the coordination. Show up every morning.
choices.result: You wake an hour earlier every day and keep a small notebook of names and times. The route runs. Women who could not have walked the distance make it to work. Your own mornings are brutal, but nobody misses a shift because of you.

choices.text: Volunteer yourself but let others sort the details.
choices.result: You put your name forward. The coordination is messier than it should be — twice a woman waits in the cold — but the carpool runs most days. Partial effort, partial result.

choices.text: Decline. You cannot take on one more thing.
choices.result: Someone else steps up eventually. Your sister notices you came home earlier and made supper. She asks no questions. A small gift to the people in your own house.

trivia: The MIA organized a carpool of over 300 cars to ferry boycotters across Montgomery throughout the protest.
Commissioner Clyde Sellers pressured the city to arrest carpool drivers on trumped-up traffic charges to break the transportation network.

events.title: Officer at the Corner
events.text: A Montgomery police officer stops you on your walk to ask where you are going and why you are not on the bus. Commissioner Sellers has instructed police to intimidate walkers. The officer is not violent, but his meaning is clear.

choices.text: Give your name, your employer, and nothing else.
choices.result: You are polite and exact. You do not explain yourself. He writes something and lets you pass. Three women watching from a stoop see what you did — stood still, stayed quiet, did not buckle.

choices.text: Say your employer needs you. Make it about work, not the boycott.
choices.result: He nods and waves you past. A true answer and an incomplete one. You arrive on time; Mrs. Hartley does not hear anything worrying today. You feel both relief and a faint unease.

choices.text: Apologize and take the bus today. Just this once.
choices.result: You step onto the bus and sit down. The driver does not look at you. At your stop, you pass two women from your church walking together in the cold. They see you in the window.

trivia: Commissioner Clyde Sellers publicly joined the White Citizens Council during the boycott and directed police to harass Black pedestrians and carpool drivers.
Mass arrests of boycott participants, including Dr. King, were intended to intimidate the community into ending the protest.

sageAdvice.name: Commissioner Clyde Sellers
sageAdvice.line: Keep this up and we'll find a reason to charge every one of you. The law has patience.

events.title: The Night of the Bombing
events.text: A bomb explodes on Dr. King's porch on January 30, 1956. His wife and daughter are inside; neither is hurt. By midnight, hundreds of armed Black men are in the street outside the house. King speaks from the broken porch and asks everyone to go home in peace.

choices.text: Go to the street. Be counted among those who showed up.
choices.result: You stand in that crowd and hear King's voice carry over the dark — 'We must love our white brothers. We must meet hate with love.' You go home at two in the morning. Your sister was awake the whole time, waiting and afraid for you.

choices.text: Stay home. Pray. Keep the children inside.
choices.result: You keep the lights low and the children quiet. The street sounds terrifying from inside. By morning you learn no one was hurt, and King spoke beautifully. You were not there, but your family slept.

choices.text: Stand in the crowd but slip away before King speaks.
choices.result: You are there long enough to feel the anger and fear in the air. You leave before the speech. Neighbors remember you were present; you do not carry the whole night with you.

trivia: King's house was bombed on January 30, 1956. He appealed to the crowd from the damaged porch to respond with love, not violence.
The bombing failed to break the boycott — the crowd's restraint that night became one of the movement's defining demonstrations of nonviolent discipline.

events.title: November 1956 — The Supreme Court Rules
events.text: The Supreme Court has declared Montgomery's bus segregation unconstitutional. The boycott is nearly over — but the MIA asks everyone to hold the line until the court order is formally delivered and buses are actually integrated. Your employer is pressing hard now; she says she needs certainty from you about whether you are coming back regularly. And your sister needs money for a medical bill this month.

choices.text: Hold the boycott to the last day. Tell Mrs. Hartley you will return when the buses are right.
choices.result: You walk every remaining day until the federal order arrives. Your sister's medical bill waits, and she does not hide that it hurts. Mrs. Hartley finds a temporary arrangement. When you finally board that integrated bus, you know you finished what you started — but the cost to your family is real, and they know it too.

choices.text: Return to the bus quietly. Your sister's bill cannot wait and the ruling is already won.
choices.result: You step onto the bus before the formal order arrives. The seat you sit in is still technically segregated. Women who know you see it; nothing is said to your face. Your sister gets her payment and the relief on her face is unmistakable. You told yourself the fight was won — and it almost was.

choices.text: Ask the MIA what to do and follow their guidance exactly.
choices.result: The MIA tells you to hold. You hold. It is not your hardest choice — you let someone else carry the weight of deciding — but you are on the right side of it when the order comes.

trivia: On November 13, 1956, the Supreme Court upheld a lower court ruling that Montgomery's bus segregation was unconstitutional.
The MIA asked boycotters to continue until the written order was received and desegregated service actually began — December 20, 1956.

sageAdvice.name: Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.
sageAdvice.role: President of the Montgomery Improvement Association
sageAdvice.line: We have come too far to let somebody else's clock tell us when we are finished.

events.title: Month Two — Mrs. Hartley learns from a neighbor that nearly every domestic on the block has been walking for the boycott. She brings it up again in the kitchen, this time with a different tone: quieter, more searching.

text.default: Mrs. Hartley looks at you for a long moment and then looks away. She does not fire you. She does not thank you. She simply begins talking about what she needs pressed by Friday, as though the conversation two weeks ago settled something she has been sitting with ever since. You are still here, still paid, still tired — but you are here as yourself, and both of you know it now.

variants.text: Mrs. Hartley looks at you for a long moment and then looks away. She does not fire you. She does not thank you. She simply begins talking about what she needs pressed by Friday, as though the conversation two weeks ago settled something she has been sitting with ever since. You are still here, still paid, still tired — but you are here as yourself, and both of you know it now.

Mrs. Hartley looks at you with something that might be relief or might be the particular comfort of not having to know. She says, 'I suspected, but I'm glad it's not a problem between us.' You say nothing. You are still here, still paid, still walking every morning before dawn — and the boycott does not know your name, and neither does she, not really. You have kept something safe and hidden something true, and you are the only one who carries both of those facts at once.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Rosa Parks
sages.title: Seamstress and NAACP Secretary
sages.bio: Rosa Parks was a seamstress and secretary of the Montgomery NAACP chapter. On December 1, 1955, she was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a Montgomery city bus — an act that triggered the 381-day boycott.
sages.greeting: You are waiting at a church door when a slight, composed woman stops beside you. She introduces herself quietly. You already know her name.
sages.advice: She speaks without drama: 'People always say I was tired — tired of giving in. I was not physically tired. I was tired of giving in. There is a difference, and it matters which one you carry with you.'

question.question: Why was Rosa Parks's arrest on December 1, 1955 considered the right moment to launch a boycott?
choices: She was a random rider with no ties to any organization
She was a respected NAACP secretary whose character could not easily be attacked
She was the first person ever arrested on a Montgomery bus

question.explanation: Civil rights leaders had been looking for the right test case. Parks was a respected, dignified NAACP secretary whose character was beyond reproach — previous candidates had been deemed too vulnerable to smear. Her arrest gave the community a symbol the opposition could not easily discredit.

verdict.good: You walked every day when walking cost something. You spoke when speaking was dangerous, organized when organizing meant less sleep and less money, and stood in that crowd the night the bombs came. The boycott succeeded — on December 20, 1956, the buses were integrated — but the women who made it possible were never written into the headline. You were one of them. You can say what you stood for, and you can say you didn't put it down.
verdict.bad: When the moment was hard you did the math, and the math said step back. The bus was there, the employer needed reassuring, the meeting could end without you. You got through the 381 days without losing your wages, and the boycott won anyway — someone else carried the weight you set down. The victory is real. Your part in it is thin. You told yourself survival was enough. Maybe it was. But the women who walked past you in the rain knew the difference, and so do you.
verdict.indifferent: You were there. You walked when it was easy, you stepped back when it cost something, and you waited for others to decide the hard questions so you could follow. The boycott happened around you — the flyers, the carpool lists, the mass meetings, the bombed porch, the Supreme Court ruling. You passed through one of the most important 381 days in American history and asked nothing of yourself that couldn't be undone by morning. History doesn't record where you stood. You would have to think hard to remember either.

data.reviewSummary:
On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks — a seamstress and secretary of the Montgomery NAACP chapter — was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a city bus. Her arrest gave the community the right moment and the right symbol: a woman whose dignity and reputation could not easily be attacked. That same night, Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council mimeographed and distributed 52,000 flyers announcing a bus boycott — before most ministers had agreed to support it. The Women's Political Council had been planning exactly this kind of protest for months.

On December 5, 1955, the first day of the boycott, nearly 40,000 Black residents refused to board city buses. That evening, a mass meeting at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church filled to overflowing. E.D. Nixon — an NAACP chapter president and Pullman porter who had bailed Parks out of jail — helped convene the meeting and pushed for organized action. The crowd chose a young pastor named Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to lead the newly formed Montgomery Improvement Association.

The MIA's initial demands were deliberate and measured: courteous treatment from drivers, first-come-first-served seating within the existing segregated sections, and Black drivers on routes serving Black neighborhoods. Full integration was not yet the stated goal. To keep the boycott running, the MIA organized a carpool network of more than 300 cars. Commissioner Clyde Sellers joined the White Citizens Council and directed police to intimidate walkers and arrest carpool drivers on false charges.

On January 30, 1956, King's house was bombed. His wife and daughter survived. Standing on the damaged porch, King urged the armed crowd to respond to hatred with love and nonviolence — a defining demonstration of the movement's discipline. The boycott held.

On November 13, 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower court ruling that Montgomery's bus segregation was unconstitutional. The MIA asked boycotters to continue until the written order arrived. Integrated bus service officially began on December 20, 1956 — 381 days after Parks's arrest. The domestic workers who walked miles every day, sacrificing wages and endurance, made the boycott's economic pressure real.

data.title: PRESSED INTO SERVICE
data.subtitle: An American Sailor in the War of 1812
data.introBody: 1811. Open water off the Atlantic coast. A Royal Navy frigate has pulled alongside your merchant vessel, and a boarding party is climbing over your rail. Your oilskin pouch holds your citizenship papers. Your wages are modest but yours. And the officer eyeing your crewmates is deciding who stays and who goes.
data.trailFeedOpener: The shadow of a Royal Navy frigate falls across your deck. The boarding party is already climbing over the rail.

events.title: The boarding — open water, 1811
events.text: A Royal Navy lieutenant moves down the line of your crewmates. One man ahead of you has already been pulled aside. The lieutenant's eye is on you. Your protection papers — certifying American citizenship — are folded inside your coat. They have saved no one yet today. The man behind you murmurs: 'Say you're from Bristol. Half these officers won't press a claimed subject. They want no paperwork.' You have seconds.

choices.text: Open your mouth and name a Bristol street you once heard a dockhand mention. Give them British birth and a vague parish. Let the claim do what the papers might not.
choices.result: He chose the self that could walk free over the self that was documented — a man who understands that identity is what you can make others believe, and who will carry the ambiguity of that transaction long after the lieutenant moves on.

choices.text: Say nothing. Draw out your protection papers and press them into the lieutenant's hands. Let the document speak. You are an American sailor and you will be recognized as one.
choices.result: He staked his person on the republic's promise and found the promise hollow — a man defined by the moment his country's word was weighed against a naval officer's convenience and found lighter.

events.title: The Talk at the Dockside Tavern
events.text: You're nursing a mug with other merchant sailors at a Baltimore waterfront tavern. The talk turns hot: the British have seized dozens of American ships under their Orders in Council, and another man claims the Navy took four of his crewmates off a brig last week. Henry Clay's War Hawks are shouting in Congress.

choices.text: Add your own story — the boarding you survived.
choices.result: The room goes quiet listening. Three other men nod — they were there too. Your voice joins a chorus that's getting harder to ignore.

choices.text: Stay quiet. It's dangerous talk.
choices.result: You keep your head down and listen. Safer, maybe. The men around you look a little disappointed.

choices.text: Tell them war is bad for merchant business.
choices.result: A man slaps the table: 'Our shipmates are in the King's navy and you're worried about your purse?' You drink alone the rest of the evening.

trivia: The Orders in Council were British rules that blocked American ships from trading with France.
Henry Clay led the War Hawks — congressmen who pushed Madison toward war in 1812.

events.title: War Is Declared — June 1812
events.text: Word reaches port: President Madison has asked Congress to declare war, and they have. The bill passed narrowly — the country is divided. Recruiting agents are on every wharf, and your merchant captain says the Royal Navy will be hunting American vessels in earnest now.

choices.text: Get your papers re-witnessed by the U.S. consul immediately.
choices.result: It costs you, but the consul stamps and signs. Your papers are as solid as they can be made. That's something.

choices.text: Sign on with an American privateer — better pay, more risk.
choices.result: The prize money is real. So is the exhaustion. Your wife's last letter asked when you were coming home. You don't have an answer.

choices.text: Lie low in port until things settle.
choices.result: Safe, and you spend a week at home. Your wages thin fast without work. The harbor is quieter, but the war is not waiting for you.

trivia: Madison cited impressment and the Orders in Council as the main causes of war in his war message to Congress.
Congress voted for war in June 1812 — the vote was closer than any previous U.S. war declaration.

events.title: Washington Is Burning — August 1814
events.text: You're ashore in a Maryland port when the sky to the west turns orange. British troops under Admiral Cockburn have marched into Washington and put the torch to the Capitol, the President's House, and the Navy Yard. Refugees fill the roads. A woman says she saw Dolley Madison loading a wagon with a portrait of Washington.

choices.text: Help the refugees moving north — carry what you can.
choices.result: You haul an old man's trunk two miles in the August heat. He tells you he worked in the Treasury. You don't ask what he saved. You both know what was lost.

choices.text: Get your ship's papers and gear secured before looters arrive.
choices.result: Smart move, maybe. Your papers are safe. The road behind you is full of people with nothing left to secure.

choices.text: Find a place to wait it out — the British won't stay long.
choices.result: You're right — they leave within twenty-six hours. But the Capitol's blackened walls stand as proof of what the young republic could not yet defend.

trivia: British forces under Admiral Cockburn burned the Capitol, the White House, and the Navy Yard on August 24–25, 1814.
Dolley Madison saved a Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington before fleeing the White House.

events.title: Blockaded in the Bay
events.text: Cockburn's squadron has blockaded the Chesapeake. No American merchant vessel moves without risk. Your captain says the British are impressing any man they catch with tar on his hands, papers or not. You need to get a message through to your family — and somehow stay useful.
events.leaveText: Stay put and wait for the blockade to ease.

attempts.buttonText: Try to slip a dispatch boat past at night.
attempts.successText: You make it through. Your message reaches home, and you learn your family is safe.
attempts.failureText: A British cutter spots you. They board, rough you up, and confiscate your oilskin pouch.

attempts.buttonText: Pay a local waterman who knows the inlets.
attempts.successText: He knows every creek and tidal flat. Message delivered, papers intact.
attempts.failureText: He takes your money and disappears. You are no better off and lighter in the purse.

events.title: The Bombardment — September 13, 1814
events.text: The British fleet opens on Fort McHenry. From the deck of a flag-of-truce vessel anchored in the harbor, a lawyer named Francis Scott Key watches through the night. So do you. For twenty-five hours the rockets and bombs fall. At dawn, the massive American flag is still flying.

choices.text: Help carry ammunition to the fort's defenders before the bombardment starts.
choices.result: You make two runs through the dark, heart hammering. A sergeant shakes your hand. At dawn the flag is still there, and you helped keep it so.

choices.text: Stay aboard the truce vessel — you're safer and can witness everything.
choices.result: You watch the rockets' red glare and the bombs bursting through the night. Key is scribbling on the back of a letter by the first gray light.

choices.text: Use the chaos to recover confiscated papers from a British tender.
choices.result: You find the tender, and you find your papers. The risk was real and you took it for yourself alone — but the flag is still flying when you climb back aboard.

trivia: The bombardment of Fort McHenry on September 13–14, 1814 lasted about 25 hours.
Francis Scott Key was detained on a British ship during the bombardment and wrote 'The Star-Spangled Banner' after seeing the flag still flying at dawn.

events.title: Peace — and What You Carry Home
events.text: The Treaty of Ghent is signed in December 1814, and news reaches America in February 1815. The war is over — no territory changed hands, impressment was not formally banned. You are alive. Your papers are what they are. Now you must decide what this war meant to you, and what you owe.

choices.text: Go straight home to your family before taking any new work.
choices.result: Your wife opens the door before you knock. The wages thin fast, but for two weeks the war is somewhere else.

choices.text: Take an immediate berth — the merchant lanes are open again and you need the money.
choices.result: You're at sea again inside a week. Your youngest doesn't recognize your face when you finally come home six months later. The money is real. So is that.

choices.text: Stay in port and speak at the sailors' gathering about what you saw.
choices.result: Men who were never pressed listen. A few who were pressed listen harder. You don't know what it changes. You say it anyway.

trivia: The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, ended the War of 1812 with no territorial changes and no formal ban on impressment.
British impressment of American sailors largely stopped after the war — not because of the treaty, but because the Napoleonic Wars had ended and Britain no longer needed the manpower.

events.title: After Fort McHenry — the flag is still there, word reaches the fleet

text.default: The news travels mouth to mouth across the dock: the fort held, the flag flew through the bombardment, the British withdrew. Around you men are moved to tears. You are moved too — but the feeling is complicated in a way you cannot explain to them. You know what it cost you to survive long enough to hear this. You wonder whether the country whose flag flew that night would have claimed you, or whether it would have weighed you the same way the lieutenant did — and found you negotiable.

sages.name: Dolley Madison
sages.title: First Lady of the United States

data.historicalContext: The War of 1812 ended with the Treaty of Ghent in December 1814, ratified by the U.S. Senate in February 1815. No territory changed hands and impressment was never formally banned — yet the war ended with American sovereignty intact and national identity galvanized. The defense of Fort McHenry produced the poem that became the national anthem. Impressment of American sailors effectively ceased after 1815 because the Napoleonic Wars that had driven British manpower demands were over. The republic had survived its second conflict with Britain, and the generation that fought it knew what they had held.

verdict.good: You held onto who you were — not just the papers, but what they stood for. When the choice was between safety and something harder, you took the harder thing, not every time, but when it counted. The war ended with no formal ban on impressment and no territory gained. The republic survived. You did too, and the men around you knew whose side you'd been on when it was uncertain. That is the only record that mattered in 1815.
verdict.bad: You got through it. Every time a choice appeared you found the one that kept your purse a little heavier and your skin a little safer. You were not cruel — you were careful, and careful is its own kind of choice. The war ended the same way for everyone: no territory, no formal promise from Britain, no clear winner. The men who held the line at Fort McHenry and the docks of Baltimore did it without much help from you. You were there. You just weren't there for them.
verdict.indifferent: The war moved through you without leaving much of a mark. You kept your head down when the talk got dangerous, waited when waiting was easier, and found the door whenever the room demanded something. Impressment, the burning of Washington, the rockets over Fort McHenry — you witnessed all of it from a comfortable distance. History did not record where you stood in those years. Neither could you, really. You passed through the founding of an idea and let someone else do the founding.

data.reviewSummary:
The War of 1812 began with grievances that had been building for years. Britain's Orders in Council blocked American ships from trading with Napoleonic France, and the Royal Navy practiced impressment — stopping American vessels and forcing sailors into British service under the doctrine that anyone born a British subject remained one for life. American citizenship papers, called protection papers, offered some defense, but British officers routinely dismissed them. Henry Clay of Kentucky led the War Hawks in Congress, arguing that American honor and sovereignty demanded a military response. President Madison cited impressment and trade interference in his war message, and Congress voted for war in June 1812 — the closest vote for any war declaration in American history, reflecting a genuinely divided nation.

The early years brought humiliation. In August 1814, British forces under Rear Admiral George Cockburn marched into Washington and burned the Capitol, the White House, and the Navy Yard. First Lady Dolley Madison stayed until the last moment, directing the rescue of the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington and key state papers before fleeing. The republic's capital lay in ruins.

Baltimore was next. On September 13–14, 1814, the British fleet bombarded Fort McHenry for roughly twenty-five hours. The fort held. At dawn, the large American garrison flag was still flying. Francis Scott Key, a Washington lawyer who had gone to negotiate a prisoner's release and been detained on a British ship during the attack, wrote 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' watching the flag survive the night. Set to music, it became 'The Star-Spangled Banner.'

The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, ended the war with no territorial changes and no formal ban on impressment. British impressment of American sailors stopped in practice after 1815 — not because the treaty required it, but because the Napoleonic Wars that had driven British manpower demands were over. The republic had survived, its identity sharpened by what it had endured.

data.title: THE THIRD CRUSADE
data.subtitle: Acre to Jerusalem, 1191–1192
data.introBody: You have taken the cross. After months at sea and weeks of brutal siege, the walls of Acre are finally crumbling. Your coin purse is lighter than when you left England, your mail is salt-rusted, and the holy city feels both close and impossibly far. Every choice from here will cost you something.
data.trailFeedOpener: Summer 1191: the Christian host tightens its grip on Acre, and you await your lord's orders.

events.title: Acre — the days after the city's surrender, before the massacre at Ayyadieh
events.text: The garrison has surrendered and among the prisoners assigned to your guard is a Saracen officer — a man your age, wounded at the same breach where your friend died. In the weeks of the siege you have watched him from the walls; through a captured interpreter he has spoken to you with a directness no courtly enemy is supposed to have. Tonight he is feverish. He asks you, through the interpreter, whether you took the cross freely or whether your lord's expectation left you no real choice. It is the most dangerous question you have ever been asked, because you do not know the answer — and the way you respond to him will force you to find one. Richard's order is clear: the prisoners are wards of the army, their lives contingent on Saladin's ransom. Nothing requires you to engage this man as a man. Nothing forbids it either, yet.

choices.text: You answer him: 'I took it freely. That is all you need to know of me.' You turn away and do not speak to him again.
choices.result: The knight seals the vow against the pressure of the particular. He is not cruel — the answer is honest as far as he is willing to go — but he refuses to let the enemy's humanity become his problem. The vow holds because he will not test it against the man it requires him to regard as less than a full interlocutor.

choices.text: You answer him honestly: that you are no longer sure — that the road from the port to this courtyard has changed the question. You stay and talk until the fever breaks.
choices.result: The knight allows the human encounter to crack the vow's certainty. He is not abandoning his faith or his king — he stays at his post, the prisoner remains a prisoner — but something has shifted: he now knows that the sacred formula does not fully contain him, and he will carry that knowledge into every decision that follows.

events.title: Fever in the Siege Lines
events.text: Half the camp is sick. A foot soldier from your lord's retinue collapses near your tent — burning with fever, his lips cracked from weeks of bad water. The surgeon is already overwhelmed. You have coin and a horse you could send for medicine from the Genoese ships.
trivia: Disease killed more crusaders at Acre than Saracen arrows.
The Genoese and Pisan fleets supplied the crusader camp by sea.

choices.text: Spend your coin — send for medicine.
choices.result: The medicine arrives by nightfall. The man recovers enough to stand. Others notice what you spent, and for what.

choices.text: Offer him water and a prayer — nothing more.
choices.result: He survives, barely. You keep your coin. The prayer felt hollow even as you said it.

choices.text: Report the sickness to the surgeon-general.
choices.result: The surgeon-general orders better water rationing. A small step, but the camp is marginally healthier for it.

events.title: The Spoils of Acre
events.text: Acre has fallen. Your section of the wall yielded silver plate, fine cloth, and a chest of Saracen coin. Your lord expects a full accounting — but the men who fought beside you have not been paid in three months. You could quietly divide a portion among them before the count.
trivia: After Acre fell in July 1191, Philip II of France and Richard divided the city's wealth and prisoners between them.

choices.text: Report everything. Give your lord his full share.
choices.result: Your lord is pleased. You receive your proper portion. The men get nothing and they know it.

choices.text: Hold back a third — split it among the men.
choices.result: The men are quietly, fiercely grateful. If your lord notices the short count, he says nothing yet.

choices.text: Keep the silver plate yourself, report the rest.
choices.result: You are richer. You are also the sort of man who does this. You will remember it later, and not fondly.

events.title: Rearguard on the Coastal March
events.text: Richard's army marches south along the coast toward Jaffa. Saladin's cavalry harass the rearguard without pause — arrows from horseback, fast and constant. The man beside you has taken a shaft in the shoulder. If you stop to help him you will fall behind the column.
trivia: Richard's strict march discipline — keeping the column tight against the sea — was key to surviving Saracen harassment on the road to Jaffa.
Saladin used mounted archers called ghulam cavalry to harass the crusader flanks.

choices.text: Drag him to the column's edge and call for a litter.
choices.result: You are exposed for a dangerous minute. Two arrows hit your shield. He lives. Your arms ache for days.

choices.text: Tell him to hold on — press forward with the column.
choices.result: He manages to keep moving, barely. You don't look back. You both survive, but you carry the image of his face.

choices.text: Shout for a sergeant and keep your station.
choices.result: A sergeant pulls the man along. You follow orders and the column holds discipline.

events.title: Battle of Arsuf — Hold or Break?
events.text: The Hospitallers at the rear have had enough. Their master is begging to charge before Richard gives the signal. You are posted near the crossover point — you could carry the order to hold, or you could let the charge begin. If they break now they may be cut off.
trivia: At Arsuf in September 1191, Richard's disciplined march formation finally broke into a charge — and it worked, scattering Saladin's army.
The Hospitallers at Arsuf nearly charged without orders, but Richard's timing turned the battle.

choices.text: Ride hard — carry Richard's order to hold.
choices.result: You reach the Hospitaller master in time. When Richard's trumpet finally sounds, the charge is glorious and coordinated. Saladin's line shatters.

choices.text: Say nothing — let the charge go.
choices.result: The Hospitallers charge before the signal. By luck it works today. But luck is not discipline, and you know that.

choices.text: Join the charge yourself — it feels like the moment.
choices.result: You survive and the battle is won. Your horse takes a lance — you'll need coin for another. Acting on feeling cost you.

events.title: Philip of France Sails Home
events.text: Philip II has declared he is ill and is returning to France. Half the French knights he commands are now asking whether their obligation follows him or the cross. One approaches you — a good fighter, but his nerve is gone. He wants to know what you are doing.
trivia: Philip II of France left the Holy Land in August 1191, shortly after Acre fell, citing illness — but many suspected political motives.
Philip's departure left Richard as sole commander, but also weakened the crusader army significantly.

choices.text: Tell him plainly: you took a vow, and you will keep it.
choices.result: He stays. Two others nearby overhear you and stay as well. Your words cost you nothing today; they may cost you everything tomorrow.

choices.text: Say it's his choice — you won't judge him.
choices.result: He sails with Philip. The army is smaller. You wonder if your silence was mercy or cowardice.

choices.text: Suggest he stay through winter, then reassess.
choices.result: He agrees, reluctantly. He fights well at Arsuf. Whether the vow held him or your words did, you cannot say.

events.title: The Treaty — and the Road Home
events.text: Richard has signed a truce with Saladin. Jerusalem remains in Muslim hands; Christian pilgrims may visit unarmed. The army will sail home. Around you, men are already packing. A group of common soldiers — Flemish and English — have not been paid their final wages. Your purse could cover it. And your lord's courier has arrived: there is trouble at home, and your family needs you back now.
trivia: The Treaty of Jaffa, signed in September 1192, ended the Third Crusade. Jerusalem remained under Saladin's control, but Christian pilgrims were allowed to visit.
Richard left the Holy Land in October 1192, never having entered Jerusalem.

choices.text: Pay the soldiers — your family can wait a fortnight.
choices.result: The men receive their wages. They will remember the knight who paid them when the lords did not. Your family counts the days without you.

choices.text: Ride for the ships immediately — your family comes first.
choices.result: You board the first ship out. The soldiers are left unpaid. You hold your family's letter and do not look back at the dock.

choices.text: Give half your coin and sail on the second ship.
choices.result: A compromise that satisfies no one fully, and perhaps serves both a little. You leave wondering if that was wisdom or evasion.

events.title: The coastal march — after Arsuf, when the army halts and the rumour spreads that Richard is negotiating with Saladin's envoys rather than marching on Jerusalem

text.default: When the men around you curse the delay as betrayal, you find yourself agreeing with a coldness that surprises you. Negotiation feels like dissolution — as if every day Richard speaks to the enemy is a day the vow loses its shape. You cannot explain this feeling to the priest who asks why your face is so hard. You know only that the vow is the last thing holding the last months together, and you will not let anyone — king, envoy, or priest — suggest it was always negotiable.

variants.text: When the men around you curse the delay as betrayal, you find yourself agreeing with a coldness that surprises you. Negotiation feels like dissolution — as if every day Richard speaks to the enemy is a day the vow loses its shape. You cannot explain this feeling to the priest who asks why your face is so hard. You know only that the vow is the last thing holding the last months together, and you will not let anyone — king, envoy, or priest — suggest it was always negotiable.

When the men around you curse the delay as betrayal, you are quieter than they expect. You think of the man in Acre whose fever broke, and you find you cannot summon the clean outrage the vow is supposed to give you. What you feel instead is something harder to name: a recognition that two men can each believe God is with them and each be telling the truth as they understand it. You do not say this aloud. You are not sure it is wisdom. You are not sure it is anything except what the road has left you with.

choices.text: Go on.

events.title: Outside Jerusalem — the second withdrawal, when Richard orders the army to turn back without making the assault

text.default: The withdrawal is an amputation. You have organised everything you are around arrival at those walls, and the order to turn back does not feel like strategy — it feels like the vow being broken by the one man who had the authority to keep it. You ride away facing forward, because you cannot let yourself look back at what you came all this way not to reach. The vow is still there, intact, but it is now a wound rather than a shelter.

variants.text: The withdrawal is an amputation. You have organised everything you are around arrival at those walls, and the order to turn back does not feel like strategy — it feels like the vow being broken by the one man who had the authority to keep it. You ride away facing forward, because you cannot let yourself look back at what you came all this way not to reach. The vow is still there, intact, but it is now a wound rather than a shelter.

You have known for weeks that you would not enter the city — not because you doubted Richard's generalship but because somewhere on the march you stopped believing that arrival would answer the question the Saracen officer asked you in Acre. What you mourn at the withdrawal is not the lost victory but the lost permission to stop asking. The road home will be long and you will have to carry the question all the way back to England, where no one will know what it means.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Richard I of England
sages.title: Commander of the Crusading Forces
sages.bio: Richard I — called the Lionheart — led the Third Crusade with ferocious energy. He captured Acre, defeated Saladin at Arsuf, and came within twelve miles of Jerusalem before recognizing that taking and holding the city was beyond his means.
sages.greeting: Richard is reviewing siege dispositions when he notices you. He speaks without looking up from the map.
sages.advice: "Acre will fall because we have denied it everything — water, food, relief. Saladin cannot break our lines and his garrison cannot hold. Patience and iron are the same weapon here."

question.question: Why did Richard order the execution of roughly 2,700 Saracen prisoners at Ayyadieh in August 1191?
choices: Saladin refused to fulfill the ransom terms of the surrender agreement
The prisoners attempted a mass escape from the crusader camp
Richard wanted to terrorize Saladin into surrendering Jerusalem
The prisoners were soldiers who had broken their oath of surrender
question.explanation: The garrison of Acre surrendered on terms requiring Saladin to pay a ransom, release Christian prisoners, and return the True Cross. When the deadlines passed without payment, Richard ordered the prisoners executed. The massacre shocked both sides and scarred the Crusade's moral legacy.
question.teksRef: WH.2(C) — Causes and effects of the Crusades on Christian and Muslim societies

sages.name: Conrad of Montferrat
sages.title: Claimant to the Kingdom of Jerusalem
sages.bio: Conrad of Montferrat defended Tyre against Saladin after Jerusalem fell and claimed the crown of Jerusalem against Guy of Lusignan. His assassination in 1192 — just days after the crusader barons chose him as king — remains one of the Crusade's unsolved mysteries.
sages.greeting: Conrad intercepts you near the command tent, his voice low and pointed. He does not trust easily, and he wants to know whose man you are.
sages.advice: "Guy lost Jerusalem and expects to keep his crown. The barons of Outremer know better. A king who holds Tyre is worth more than a king who lost everything else. Richard will see reason, or he will not."

question.question: What was the core dispute between Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan?
choices: Both claimed the right to be King of Jerusalem
Conrad wanted to abandon the siege of Acre, Guy wanted to continue
They disagreed over whether to accept Saladin's peace terms
Conrad supported Philip of France while Guy supported Richard
question.explanation: Guy of Lusignan had been King of Jerusalem but lost the kingdom at the Battle of Hattin in 1187. Conrad of Montferrat held Tyre and argued that Guy had forfeited the crown. The rivalry split the crusader coalition and forced Richard and Philip to broker a compromise — Guy would reign for life, then Conrad would succeed.
question.teksRef: WH.2(C) — Political fragmentation and internal conflict within the Crusader states

sages.name: Saladin
sages.title: Sultan of Egypt and Syria, Defender of Jerusalem
sages.bio: Saladin unified Egypt and Syria under Ayyubid rule, recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, and successfully held it against the Third Crusade. Renowned in both Muslim and Christian chronicles for his discipline, generosity to defeated enemies, and strategic patience.
sages.greeting: A captured Saracen courier, released under flag of truce, carries a brief message from Saladin — a question, translated by a Frankish clerk who served at his court.
sages.advice: The message reads: 'Your king is brave and his discipline is real. But he cannot hold Jerusalem even if he takes it. He knows this. The city is not the end of this road — it is where the road becomes impossible.'

question.question: How did Saladin recapture Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187, before the Third Crusade began?
choices: He defeated the main crusader army at the Battle of Hattin and the city surrendered
He bribed the defenders to open the city gates at night
He built a fleet and blockaded Jerusalem by sea
A plague inside Jerusalem killed most of the defenders before he arrived
question.explanation: Saladin lured the crusader army into waterless terrain near the Horns of Hattin and destroyed it in July 1187. Without an army, Jerusalem could not be defended and surrendered in October 1187. The fall of Jerusalem was the direct cause of the Third Crusade.

route.title: The Crusade, 1191–1192
route.description: From the siege of Acre to the truce outside Jerusalem — a year of war, endurance, and reckoning.

Acre

Supply ships sailing alongside the army

Battle of Arsuf

choices: He believed the city was too holy to attack
He lacked siege equipment
He judged he could not hold it after capturing it
Saladin offered him a generous ransom to withdraw

choices: Saladin destroyed the city of Antioch
Saladin captured Jerusalem after the Battle of Hattin
A Muslim fleet sank crusader ships in the Mediterranean
The Byzantine Emperor expelled the Franks from Constantinople
eventTrivia.fact: Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187 destroyed the crusader field army and led directly to the fall of Jerusalem, shocking Christian Europe and triggering the Third Crusade.

eventTrivia.question: What happened to the roughly 2,700 Saracen prisoners from Acre's garrison?
choices: They were enslaved and sent to Cyprus
They were exchanged for French prisoners held by Saladin
Richard ordered them executed when Saladin missed the ransom deadline
They were released on their oath to leave the Holy Land

choices: Christian knights could garrison the city walls
Unarmed Christian pilgrims could visit Jerusalem freely
The True Cross would be returned to Rome
Crusaders could keep Acre permanently
eventTrivia.fact: The treaty ending the Third Crusade permitted unarmed Christian pilgrims to visit Jerusalem — the holy sites remained accessible even though the city itself stayed in Saladin's hands.

eventTrivia.question: How did Philip II of France's early departure affect Richard's campaign?
choices: It freed Richard to negotiate directly with Saladin
It removed a significant portion of the crusader army, weakening Richard's force
It had little effect because the French troops remained behind
It allowed Richard to claim sole command of Jerusalem's throne
eventTrivia.fact: When Philip sailed home in August 1191, he took or freed many French forces — reducing the crusader army and making the eventual push on Jerusalem even harder.

eventTrivia.question: What role did the Genoese and Pisan fleets play in the crusader siege of Acre?
choices: They blockaded Acre from the sea, cutting off Saladin's supply ships
They transported siege engines overland from Antioch
They carried ransom payments between Richard and Saladin
They patrolled the Jordan River to prevent Saracen crossings
eventTrivia.fact: Italian city-state fleets — especially Genoese and Pisan ships — maintained a naval blockade of Acre's harbor, preventing Saladin from resupplying or reinforcing the garrison by sea.

eventTrivia.question: Why was Acre strategically important to the crusaders?
choices: It was the closest city to Jerusalem by land
It was the best port on the Levantine coast — a base for supplies and ships
It held the True Cross captured at Hattin
It was the residence of the Patriarch of Jerusalem
eventTrivia.fact: Acre's harbor made it the essential supply base on the Levantine coast. Controlling Acre meant controlling the sea lanes — everything the crusader army needed could flow through its port.

eventTrivia.question: What is a 'crusade' in the medieval Christian sense?
choices: A pilgrimage made on foot to Rome
A holy war authorized by the Pope, with spiritual rewards for participants
A military contract between a lord and mercenary soldiers
A trade expedition licensed by the Byzantine Emperor
eventTrivia.fact: Crusades were holy wars proclaimed by the Pope. Those who took the cross were promised indulgences — remission of sins — in exchange for their service, which made the spiritual stakes deeply personal.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Kingdom of Jerusalem before Hattin?

A crusader kingdom established after the First Crusade, ruled by a Christian king
A Byzantine province reconquered from the Seljuk Turks
A trading colony shared between Venice and Genoa
eventTrivia.fact: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was founded after the First Crusade in 1099. It was a feudal Christian state that controlled Jerusalem and much of the Levantine coast until Saladin's victory at Hattin.

eventTrivia.question: What does 'taking the cross' mean for a medieval knight?

Being knighted by a bishop in a religious ceremony
Purchasing a relic of the True Cross as a talisman
Signing a military contract with Richard's household
eventTrivia.fact: To 'take the cross' meant publicly vowing to go on crusade — the knight literally sewed a cloth cross onto his surcoat. Breaking this vow was considered a serious spiritual offense.

data.historicalContext: The Third Crusade (1189–1192) was launched after Saladin captured Jerusalem following his victory at the Battle of Hattin in 1187. Richard I and Philip II of France led the Christian coalition, capturing Acre in July 1191 after a grinding two-year siege. Richard won a tactical victory at Arsuf and marched to within twelve miles of Jerusalem — twice — but withdrew both times, judging the city could not be held. The campaign ended with the Treaty of Jaffa in September 1192: Jerusalem remained under Saladin's control, but unarmed Christian pilgrims were permitted to visit. Richard left the Holy Land in October 1192, never having entered Jerusalem. The Third Crusade is remembered as a military near-success and a political failure — the Crusading ideal survived, but the holy city did not change hands.

verdict.good: You came to the Holy Land with a vow and you kept something harder — your conscience. You spent coin you needed, dragged wounded men out of arrows, and stayed when others sailed home. Jerusalem did not fall. Richard signed a treaty and the army packed its tents, and all the sacrifice landed not on a liberated city but on a piece of parchment. You lost what you came to win. But the men who marched beside you knew what you were, and you can say the same. That is not nothing. In 1192, it may have been everything.
verdict.bad: You calculated every choice and the math usually favored you. The coin stayed in your purse, the silver plate went quietly into your pack, and when the wounded man needed you you kept your station and told yourself that was discipline. The treaty was signed. Jerusalem stayed in Saladin's hands. You are sailing home richer than most and no more righteous than the lords who sent you. The crusade asked you who you were. You answered clearly enough. The men you left on that dock without their wages will remember the answer too.
verdict.indifferent: You were there. That is the most that can be said. Every time the road forked you found the path that asked least of you — the prayer instead of the coin, the sergeant instead of the decision, the compromise that satisfied no one and committed you to nothing. Richard signed the treaty. Jerusalem remained in Saladin's hands. Tens of thousands of people gave everything they had to this campaign, and it ended without the city. You passed through one of the most consequential military expeditions of the medieval world and it left no mark on you, because you left no mark on it.

data.reviewSummary: The Third Crusade began because Saladin — sultan of Egypt and Syria — destroyed the crusader field army at the Battle of Hattin in July 1187 and captured Jerusalem that same year. Christian Europe was shocked, and Pope Gregory VIII called for a new crusade. Richard I of England and Philip II of France answered, gathering a large coalition force and sailing to the Holy Land. The crusaders arrived to join a siege already underway outside Acre, the great port city on the Levantine coast. Acre mattered above all because its harbor controlled the sea lanes — every supply ship, every replacement weapon, every reinforcement had to flow through it. Genoese and Pisan fleets maintained a naval blockade of the harbor while the army pressed from land, and disease spread catastrophically through the overcrowded besieging camp, killing thousands before the walls fell. Acre surrendered in July 1191. When Saladin missed the deadlines for the ransom terms — payment, the release of Christian prisoners, and the return of the True Cross — Richard ordered the roughly 2,700 soldiers of the garrison executed at Ayyadieh. Philip II, citing illness, sailed home shortly after the city fell, taking or releasing much of the French force and significantly weakening the crusading army. Richard then marched south along the coast toward Jaffa. He kept the army tight against the sea so supply ships could provision it, enduring constant harassment from Saladin's mounted archers. At Arsuf in September 1191, Richard's disciplined infantry held formation until the charge shattered Saladin's line — the campaign's clearest battlefield victory. Richard led the army to within twelve miles of Jerusalem twice but withdrew both times. His councils judged that even if the city fell, the crusaders could not hold it once the armies went home — taking Jerusalem without the means to defend it would be meaningless. In September 1192 Richard and Saladin signed the Treaty of Jaffa: Jerusalem remained in Muslim hands, but unarmed Christian pilgrims were permitted to visit freely. Richard left the Holy Land in October 1192 without ever entering the city he had come to liberate.

data.title: ROAD WEST
data.subtitle: Oklahoma to California, 1936
data.introBody: It's 1936. The land is gone — three years of drought and the bank's patience ran out together. Everything you own is tied to the roof of the Model A. Route 66 runs west and that's the direction California is in. Load the family and go.
data.trailFeedOpener: June 1936: the family loads the last crate onto the running board and points the truck west.

events.title: Early on Route 66 — a California Agricultural Inspection Station at the Arizona border
events.text: A state inspector blocks the truck, walks slowly around it, and says loud enough for the children to hear: 'Another load of Okies. You people breed like rabbits and then expect California to feed you.' He holds your papers a long time, not reading them — just holding them, making you wait. Your youngest is asleep in the truck bed. Your oldest child, maybe ten years old, is watching your face to learn what to do. The inspector finally looks up and waits for you to answer him.

choices.text: You look at the ground and say, 'Yes sir, just looking for work, sir. We won't be any trouble.' You give him what he wants — deference, smallness — and he waves you through.
choices.result: This person has decided that the road is a place where survival requires a kind of disappearing — that protecting your family sometimes means letting someone diminish you. The choice is made with eyes open. It is a wound taken on purpose.

choices.text: You meet his eyes and say, level and quiet: 'My name is [family name]. We farmed our land for twenty years before the drought took it. We're not looking for charity — we're looking for work, same as any man.' You hold his gaze until he hands the papers back.
choices.result: This person has decided that there is something in them the road cannot have, no matter the price. The family name is spoken out loud in front of a hostile stranger and a watching child. The cost of that moment — whatever it turns out to be — is accepted.

events.title: Black Blizzard on the Panhandle
events.text: A wall of brown-black dust rolls in from the north, blocking out the noon sun. You can barely see the hood ornament. Push through and risk the engine, or stop and wait it out eating into your food.
trivia: Dust storms in the 1930s could be three hundred feet tall and turn midday into midnight.
Families stuffed wet rags under doors to keep the dust from burying everything inside.

choices.text: Stop and wait under a wet cloth.
choices.result: You sit in the dark for four hours. Ma tears up an old flour sack and soaks it so the children can breathe. The truck is fine when it clears. The crate is lighter.

choices.text: Push through slow — keep moving.
choices.result: You make ten miles blind. The air filter chokes with fine grit and you spend two dollars at a filling station in Amarillo cleaning it out. The engine coughs for a day after.

events.title: Family Broke Down by the Road
events.text: A family's Hudson is dead on the shoulder, hood up, children sitting in the dust. The father flags you down. They haven't eaten since yesterday and he's got no cash and no tools.
trivia: More than 200,000 Okies and Arkies traveled Route 66 to California between 1935 and 1940.
Breakdowns on desert stretches could strand families for days with no water nearby.

choices.text: Share food and help with the repair.
choices.result: You give them a half-loaf of cornbread and spend an hour under the hood together. They get moving. The wife presses a jar of honey into Ma's hands and won't take no for an answer.

choices.text: Give them a little food, keep moving.
choices.result: You hand over two biscuits through the window and roll on. Ma doesn't say anything. Your oldest watches the family in the side mirror until they disappear.

choices.text: Slow down but don't stop — can't risk it.
choices.result: You pass them at five miles an hour. The father's eyes find yours. You press the gas. Nobody in the truck speaks for the next fifty miles.

events.title: Radiator Boiling in the Mohave
events.text: The temperature gauge pins hard right and steam shoots from under the hood. You limp to a roadside filling station. The mechanic says the water pump is failing — a three-dollar repair or a slow death in the desert.
trivia: Model A Fords were notorious for overheating when overloaded on desert grades.
Families often carried water jugs tied to the running boards specifically for the Mohave crossing.

choices.text: Pay for the repair.
choices.result: It stings every dollar, but the pump holds all the way to Needles. You don't say it, but you know that three dollars just kept the family alive.

choices.text: Nurse it with water jugs — save the cash.

outcomes.result: You stop every ten miles to pour water in the radiator. Slow, hot, miserable. You make it, barely.
The pump seizes twelve miles out of Needles. A passing trucker charges you eight dollars to tow you in. Now you've spent more and lost a day.

events.title: The Roadside Camp at Needles
events.text: Twenty families are camped under cottonwoods at the river. A woman is organizing everyone to share supper — one pot of beans, everyone puts something in. A man with a guitar plays quietly. This is the first real rest in days.
trivia: Government and charity roadside camps provided minimal shelter but crucial community for migrant families.
Dorothea Lange photographed many of these camps for the Farm Security Administration in 1936-1937.

sageAdvice.name: Dorothea Lange
sageAdvice.line: These camps are where dignity lives. People look out for each other here.

choices.text: Put the last of the salt pork in the pot.
choices.result: You get more back than you put in. The children eat a full meal. Ma laughs for the first time since Oklahoma. You sleep better than you have in weeks.

choices.text: Eat by yourselves — protect the crate.
choices.result: You sit at the edge of the firelight and eat separately. The other families notice. The woman with the pot doesn't say anything, but she stops calling over.

choices.text: Add a little flour — play it safe.
choices.result: You contribute enough to belong without giving much. Nobody says anything. You eat at the fire and the evening passes quietly.

events.title: We Don't Serve Your Kind Here
events.text: You pull into a small California town for bread. The store owner sees the Oklahoma plates, the loaded truck, the dust. He says the store is closed. It isn't. Two local men lean against the wall watching.
trivia: California passed laws restricting migrants from entering, and some counties used 'bum blockades' to turn back cars with out-of-state plates.
The word 'Okie' became a slur in California regardless of which state a migrant actually came from.

choices.text: Buy at the next town and say nothing.
choices.result: You find a store fifteen miles on that sells to you without comment. The children don't ask questions. Your oldest has learned something today that you didn't teach.

choices.text: Say your name clearly and ask again.
choices.result: You say your name and where you're from and that your money is as good as anyone's. He doesn't sell to you. You leave without bread. But your oldest heard you say your name like it meant something.

events.title: The Contractor's Terms
events.text: The labor camp boss offers work — picking peaches at two cents a box. There are fifty families waiting for the same twenty spots. A man beside you whispers that last week's pickers organized to demand three cents and got thrown off the property. The boss is watching you both.
events.imageSearchQuery: California Central Valley labor camp 1930s migrants
trivia: California's Central Valley farm labor contractors hired migrants at the lowest possible wages, knowing desperate families had no bargaining power.
Migrants who organized for better wages were often blacklisted from entire counties.

choices.text: Take the two cents and say nothing.
choices.result: You work six days. Your back holds. The children eat. You don't look the other man in the eye when he doesn't get a spot. The money is real and it buys another week.

choices.text: Stand with the man and ask for three cents.
choices.result: The boss marks you both down and moves on to the next family. No work today, maybe not tomorrow. The man shakes your hand. Your oldest asks why you did it. You tell them: because two cents is not what the work is worth and you know it.

choices.text: Step away from him before the boss sees.
choices.result: You get a spot. He doesn't. You work three days before the contractor cuts the crew again. You didn't lose anything today, and you didn't gain anything either.

sages.name: Hugh Hammond Bennett
sages.title: Chief, Soil Conservation Service

Congress funded the Soil Conservation Service that day.

sages.advice: He listens to you describe the land going to dust. 'Deep plowing broke the sod that held the soil for ten thousand years. One drought and the wind took it all. That's not bad luck — that's a mistake we made and can fix, if anyone will listen.'

data.historicalContext: Between 1935 and 1940, an estimated 2.5 million people fled the Dust Bowl states for California. Most arrived to find wages far below what recruiters had promised, hostile locals, and labor camps that barely provided shelter. California growers deliberately maintained an oversupply of desperate workers to keep wages near starvation levels. The federal government's Farm Security Administration built a small number of sanitary camps and sent photographers to document the crisis, but meaningful relief was slow and incomplete. The Dust Bowl migration became one of the largest internal displacements in American history — and the families who made it did not find the promised land waiting.

verdict.good: You protected your family and held your name intact at the same time — not always, not without cost, but enough. You shared food when you had little. You said your name in a store that wouldn't have you. You stood next to a man asking for a fair wage when it was easier to step away. The strike was broken. The wages stayed low. Most families on that road got less than they deserved, and so did you. But you arrived in California as the same person who left Oklahoma. That is harder than it sounds, and rarer than the history books suggest.
verdict.bad: You got through. Every time the choice came, you took the one that kept the coffee tin heavier and the crate fuller, and let someone else pay the difference. You drove past the family on the shoulder. You stepped away from the man at the labor gate. You ate by yourself at the edge of the firelight. The crops got picked, the contractors kept their margins, and the wages stayed at two cents a box. You were on the surviving side of that calculation. The people you left behind on each of those shoulders are still there in the history. You passed them going the other direction.
verdict.indifferent: You drove the road and you arrived. You took the easy call every time it surfaced — not because you were cruel, but because it was there and the hard call was not required of you. The dust storms happened. The border guards happened. The labor camps happened. You moved through all of it without it asking much, because you made sure it didn't. Two and a half million people made this drive. Most of them had no choice about being on the road. You had choices at every stop. You spent most of them on the exit.

data.reviewSummary:
In the 1930s, a decade of drought combined with decades of deep plowing that had destroyed the native grasslands holding the Southern Plains topsoil in place. When the rains stopped, the exposed soil blew away in massive dust storms — the Black Blizzards that turned midday into night. Tenant farming families, who paid a share of their harvest as rent and had no savings to survive a failed crop, were the first and hardest hit. Banks foreclosed, landowners evicted, and mechanized tractors made tenant labor unnecessary even on land that might have recovered. By 1935, families were loading everything onto overloaded cars and trucks and pointing them west on Route 66 — the highway that ran from Oklahoma through Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona into California.

An estimated 2.5 million people made that migration. Californians called them all 'Okies,' using the word as a slur regardless of which state the family actually came from. Some counties set up bum blockades — checkpoints at the state line to turn away cars with out-of-state plates. Those who got through found labor contractors in the Central Valley offering fifty cents to a dollar a day picking fruit, knowing that the oversupply of desperate families made any wage acceptable.

Hugh Hammond Bennett, chief of the federal Soil Conservation Service, argued before Congress that the Dust Bowl was not bad luck but a preventable man-made disaster caused by plowing up the native grass. The Farm Security Administration responded by funding relief programs and hiring photographers — including Dorothea Lange, whose 1936 images of migrant families in California camps brought the human cost of the crisis to national attention.

John Steinbeck spent months in those camps before publishing The Grapes of Wrath in 1939. The novel followed the fictional Joad family from Oklahoma to California and won the Pulitzer Prize, shaping how Americans understood the migration for generations. California growers tried to ban it; Eleanor Roosevelt publicly defended it. The migrant camps survived largely through mutual aid — families pooling food, labor, and care because federal relief was slow and banking credit was unavailable to them.
